title: Quant Foundry
tagline: An adversarial research lab for trading strategies: deterministic walk-forward backtests on synthetic markets, a sealed holdout, explicit costs, and rejections published as prominently as wins.
note: Every price series is synthetic, generated from a committed seed. Nothing here is market data, no broker is connected, and no profit is claimed.
problem: Most backtests flatter their author: the strategy is tuned on the same data it is scored on, costs are left out, and the losers quietly disappear. The question here is whether a research lab can be built so that cheating is structurally hard: every experiment recorded, the final test data sealed before any strategy sees it, fees and slippage charged, and a rejection treated as a result worth publishing.
built:
A Python research engine plus a GitHub-native harness and a static React site:

  • Synthetic markets: a seeded price generator and bounded CSV ingestion with validation, so every run is reproducible.
  • Three strategy families: trend, mean reversion and volatility breakout, each with a small parameter grid.
  • An event-driven simulator: signal on the close, fill at the next open, with fees, slippage and position limits.
  • Walk-forward selection with a sealed holdout: parameters are chosen on rolling windows, then scored once on data that was locked away, with sensitivity analysis, benchmarks and a verdict.
  • A GitHub-native harness: run requests arrive as issues, results live on a state branch, and an outcome loop keeps memory across runs.
  • A public site with in-browser cost sensitivity, built with React, Vite, TypeScript, GSAP and Lenis.

steps.title: Generate markets nobody can overfit to by memory
steps.body: Prices are synthetic, generated from a committed seed on a Monday to Friday calendar. That removes any chance of a strategy "knowing" a famous crash, and it means the adversarial check can run on pure random walks, where any accepted strategy is a false positive by definition.

steps.title: Simulate like a broker would charge you
steps.body: The simulator is event-driven: a signal computed on the close fills at the next open, never the same bar. Fees and a fixed slippage are charged on every trade and position limits are enforced, so a strategy that only works with free, instant fills does not survive.

steps.title: Seal the holdout, then select walk-forward
steps.body: A final slice of each series is sealed before any strategy runs. Parameters are chosen on rolling in-sample windows and checked on the following out-of-sample window; only the surviving configuration is scored once on the holdout. A t-statistic rule on the result decides accept or reject.

steps.title: Publish rejections, not just wins
steps.body: Every experiment is recorded on the state branch with a release record in releases/current.json. Verdicts, sensitivity tables and benchmarks are shown for rejected strategies with the same prominence as accepted ones.

steps.title: Run everything through GitHub
steps.body: A run is requested by opening a Research run request issue form. The owner's requests run automatically on Actions; anyone else's wait for a job:approved label. Locally the same engine runs with one command.
steps.code:
uv sync --frozen
uv run python -m quantfoundry run --request req.json --out out/

steps.title: Prove the replay is byte-identical
steps.body: Same-machine byte-identical replay is a release gate. One request was also replayed across macOS and GitHub's Ubuntu runner: every analytic output matched byte for byte, and the only difference was the gzip container of dataset.csv.gz, whose decompressed content still matched the sha256 in manifest.json.

results:
• Adversarial check: on pure random walks, 1 of 30 default-size runs accepted a strategy. The t-statistic rule cut false acceptances sharply but does not remove them.
  • Cross-platform replay: every analytic output byte-identical between macOS and Ubuntu for the one request tested; the dataset archive differed only in its gzip container.
  • Release gate: same-machine byte-identical replay is required before a release record is published.

The README publishes no return, Sharpe or win-rate figures, and that is the point: daily bars make Sharpe estimates noisy, and the lab's job is to reject strategies, not to advertise them.
next:
• Add holidays, corporate actions and a market-impact model beyond fixed slippage.
  • Allow short positions and widen the strategy grids once the false-acceptance rate is better characterised.
  • Run the optional AI grader once an inference secret is configured, and record in each release whether it ran.
